options.text: The waits grow, the calls thin out, and the run recovers when the provider does.
options.why: Tempting. That is what backoff does, but this harness waits the same 200 ms every time.

options.text: It sends about thirty calls into the outage, one every half second, and ends with error.
options.why: Right. The wait stays at 200 ms, so each try takes about half a second, and the run stops after the thirtieth call.

options.text: It switches to a larger model and succeeds.
options.why: Tempting. The overload is on the provider's side, and a larger model does not change that.

outcome: It made thirty calls in about fifteen seconds, every one overloaded, and ended as error. The outage was still going.
question: The provider is overloaded at the start. The harness retries, but it waits the same 200 ms after each failure, and the outage lasts 20 seconds. What happens?

options.why: Tempting. The overloaded error is transient: the API says it is temporarily overloaded, so a retry can succeed.

options.text: An invalid request, a format or content problem.
options.why: Right. A 400 carries invalid_request_error for a request format or content problem. The same request fails the same way.
Tempting. A timeout means the request did not finish in time, which a later try may fix.

question: Which error is a permanent error, the kind a retry never fixes?

options.text: The retries spread out on their own, so nothing more is needed.
options.why: Tempting. Identical waits keep the clients in step, so they retry together again.

options.text: They retry together again and load the provider at the same moments.
options.why: Right. Without jitter, the same wait sends every retry at once. Jitter spreads them out.

options.text: The provider rejects all ten retries for good.
options.why: Tempting. The provider can recover; the problem is the crowd of retries arriving at once.

question: Ten clients fail at the same moment and retry with the same backoff and no jitter. What happens?

options.text: It sends the call anyway, and counts it as a retry.
options.why: Tempting. The point of an open breaker is that it does not send more calls at a failing provider.

options.text: It holds the call back for the cooldown, then lets a call through again.
options.why: Right. The breaker stops retries from adding load while the provider recovers.

options.text: It ends the whole run for good.
options.why: Tempting. The breaker holds calls back for a cooldown. It does not end the run.

question: A circuit breaker opens after three failures in a row. What does an open breaker do with the next call?

options.text: Nothing. A failed tool is hidden from the model so it does not get confused.
options.why: Tempting. The model cannot correct a mistake it never sees.

options.text: The error text as a tool result, marked as an error.
options.why: Right. is_error is set to true when the tool execution resulted in an error, so the model knows the call failed and why.

options.text: A generic success message, so the run keeps moving.
options.why: Tempting. A false success hides the error, and the model builds on it.

question: A tool fails, and its error text is the only thing the model sees. What should the harness send back?

options.text: Retrying less often, so the action is less likely to repeat.
options.why: Tempting. Fewer retries does not stop a repeat. The request must say it is the same request.

options.text: An idempotency key sent with the request, so a repeat is recognised and not run twice.
options.why: Right. A repeated request with the same key has the same effect as the first one.
Tempting. A longer wait does not change what the server does with a repeated request.

question: A retry might run an action twice, such as a charge. What makes the retry safe?
